title: Soft law with hard consequences
subtitle: The UK Corporate Governance Code and 'comply or explain'
objectives: Explain the 'comply or explain' mechanism and why the Code binds premium listed companies without being enacted as statute
Identify the 2024 Code's core provisions on board effectiveness, audit/risk oversight and remuneration, and the new Provision 29 on internal controls monitoring
Distinguish a hard statutory duty (such as CA 2006 s 172) from a soft governance norm enforced through disclosure rather than direct legal liability

leadingAuthorities.role: The current Code; applies on a 'comply or explain' basis to premium listed companies via the FCA Listing Rules
New requirement for the board to monitor, and declare on the effectiveness of, the company's risk management and internal control framework
The hard statutory duty to promote the success of the company — the legal baseline the Code's soft norms sit on top of

whyThisMattersTemplate.default: Students often assume that if it's written down with numbered provisions, it must be law. It isn't, and that distinction is the spine of this lesson. Where the profile shows knowledge is ahead of application, this brief note appears: 'You can name the Code's sections — this lesson checks whether you can tell a listed company what actually happens if it ignores one.'

profileHooks.weakApplication: You've scored well on recall here before. Expect scenario questions asking what a company must disclose, not just what the Code says in the abstract.
profileHooks.weakKnowledge: Start with Part 1 and be precise about what 'comply or explain' actually requires — everything else in this lesson, including Provision 29's phasing, depends on getting that mechanism right first.

overview.hook: No statute compels a listed company to hold regular board evaluations, to keep its remuneration committee independent, or — from 2026 — to formally review its own internal controls. Nothing in the Companies Act says any of that must happen. And yet every premium listed company in the UK does almost all of it, in detail, every year. This lesson is about a strange and effective kind of law: rules with no direct legal force, backed by a market that punishes companies who admit they aren't following them.
overview.lawStatedNotice: Provision 29 of the UK Corporate Governance Code 2024 only takes effect for accounting periods beginning on or after 1 January 2026 — it is phasing in, not yet settled market practice, and this lesson teaches it on that basis. Law stated as at 23 September 2026; check current FRC guidance for the latest position on implementation, since the FRC continues to publish supporting material as the first affected reporting cycles approach.

parts.heading: A code with no teeth of its own
parts.voice: argumentative — states the puzzle, then resolves it
body: The UK Corporate Governance Code is issued by the Financial Reporting Council (FRC), a regulator, not Parliament. Breaching it is not a breach of any statute, and a company that ignores every provision in it commits no offence under the Code itself. On paper, that should make it close to irrelevant.

It isn't, because the Code's force comes from somewhere else entirely: the FCA's Listing Rules require every company with a premium listing on the London Stock Exchange to include, in its annual report, a statement of how it has applied the Code's Principles, and either confirm it has complied with each Provision or explain, specifically and meaningfully, why it hasn't. That disclosure obligation is a hard legal requirement, enforced through the Listing Rules; the underlying governance conduct it reports on is not.

This is 'comply or explain' — the UK's alternative to a rigid, one-size-fits-all statutory governance code. A company can lawfully depart from any Provision. What it cannot lawfully do is stay silent about it, or offer an explanation so thin it fails to actually inform investors why the departure is justified for that company.

components.definition: The UK's governance regulatory model: premium listed companies are not legally required to comply with each Provision of the Code, but the FCA Listing Rules do legally require them to disclose whether they complied, and to give a clear, specific explanation for any departure.

interaction.prompt: Is it a breach of the FCA Listing Rules for a premium listed company to simply not comply with a Provision of the UK Corporate Governance Code?
options: No — provided it discloses the departure and gives a proper explanation
Yes — every Provision must be complied with by law
interaction.feedbackCorrect: Right. Non-compliance itself is lawful under 'comply or explain' — the legal requirement is the disclosure and explanation, not compliance with the underlying Provision.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Not quite. The Listing Rules do not compel compliance with any given Provision — they compel disclosure of compliance or a proper explanation for departing from it. The Code's substance is soft; the disclosure duty around it is hard.

parts.heading: What the Code actually asks for: board effectiveness
parts.voice: structural — a reference-style survey of the Code's core themes
body: The 2024 Code is organised around five broad areas: board leadership and company purpose, division of responsibilities, composition/succession/evaluation, audit/risk/internal control, and remuneration. Board effectiveness runs through several of these strands at once, and it's the theme examiners return to most often because it tests whether a student understands governance as an ongoing process, not a one-off compliance checklist.

The recurring expectations are: a chair who is independent on appointment and leads a board with a clear balance of executive and independent non-executive directors; regular formal evaluation of the board, its committees and individual directors, with external facilitation of that evaluation periodically rather than every year; and proper succession planning so that leadership change doesn't destabilise the company. None of these are legal requirements in the Companies Act sense — a company that skips a board evaluation commits no offence — but skipping one, and then explaining why, is a disclosure a company has to be able to defend to its own shareholders.

The through-line across the whole Code, and worth holding onto for every Provision that follows, is that 'comply or explain' assumes shareholders, not regulators, are the primary enforcers. A weak explanation doesn't attract a fine; it attracts a difficult AGM, a shareholder revolt on a resolution, or a falling share price.

components.label: Board effectiveness, at a glance
points: Independent chair on appointment, balancing executive and non-executive strength on the board
Regular formal board and committee evaluation, with periodic external facilitation
Clear succession planning for the chair, chief executive and senior leadership
None of this is a Companies Act obligation — the sanction for weak practice is shareholder and market reaction to a poor 'explain', not legal liability

interaction.prompt: Tap the sentence from this annual report extract that is a compliant 'explain', rather than a bare non-compliance statement.
interaction.scenarioText: The company did not conduct an externally facilitated board evaluation this year. This is because the board commissioned a full external evaluation eighteen months ago, has substantially implemented its recommendations, and judged an internally led follow-up review a more proportionate use of board time this year, with the next externally facilitated evaluation scheduled for next year in line with the Code's expected cycle.
tappableSpans: did not conduct an externally facilitated board evaluation this year
commissioned a full external evaluation eighteen months ago
judged an internally led follow-up review a more proportionate use of board time
next externally facilitated evaluation scheduled for next year
interaction.correctSpan: judged an internally led follow-up review a more proportionate use of board time
interaction.feedbackCorrect: That's the substantive reasoning — it tells shareholders why the departure was a considered, proportionate choice for this board in this year, which is what a proper 'explain' requires. The other spans are just the facts around it; this is the actual justification.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Look for the sentence that gives a reason, not just a fact. A compliant 'explain' has to justify the departure to shareholders, not merely narrate what did or didn't happen and when the next review is scheduled.

parts.heading: Audit, risk and remuneration: where the Code gets specific
parts.voice: structural — moves from board culture to the mechanics regulators watch most closely
body: The audit, risk and internal control section is where the Code is at its most prescriptive, because this is the area most directly tied to the reliability of a company's financial statements. The expectations include an audit committee composed of independent non-executive directors, with at least one member having recent and relevant financial experience; a formal process for assessing the external auditor's independence and effectiveness; and a fair, balanced and understandable annual report — a standard the board as a whole, not just the audit committee, is expected to take responsibility for.

The remuneration section carries similar specificity: remuneration committees should be independent of executive influence, pay policies should be designed to promote long-term success rather than short-term share-price performance, and post-employment shareholding requirements and clawback/malus provisions are expected features of executive pay schemes, so that pay can be recovered if it later turns out to have been based on misstated results or misconduct.

Notice the pattern across both areas: the Code doesn't just say 'be independent' or 'be fair' in the abstract. It specifies structures (who sits on which committee), processes (how often something is reviewed) and mechanisms (clawback triggers) — which is exactly why 'comply or explain' works reasonably well here. A departure is usually easy to spot and describe precisely, which makes the explanation easy for shareholders to evaluate.

components.citation: UK Corporate Governance Code 2024, illustrative Provision language (audit committee independence)
components.text: The board should establish an audit committee of independent non-executive directors, with a minimum membership of three, or in the case of smaller companies, two. The committee as a whole shall have competence relevant to the sector in which the company operates. The chair of the board should not be a member of the audit committee.
elements: Audit committee composed of independent non-executive directors
Minimum membership (three, or two for smaller companies)
Board chair excluded from committee membership

interaction.prompt: Under the audit committee provision above, why is the board chair excluded from committee membership even though the chair is independent on appointment?
options: To keep the committee's oversight of financial reporting and the external auditor separate from the individual who leads the board's overall agenda and management relationships
Because the chair is legally barred by statute from sitting on any board committee
Because the chair lacks the financial competence required
interaction.feedbackCorrect: Right. The separation is about structural independence of oversight, not a statutory bar or a competence judgement — the audit function is meant to check the board and management, including the chair's own leadership of that relationship.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: There's no statutory bar here, and competence isn't the issue. The exclusion is designed to keep audit oversight structurally separate from the chair's own role leading the board and its relationship with management.

parts.heading: Provision 29: the internal controls reform, and why it's still phasing in
parts.voice: cautious — flags the live, unsettled edge of the material explicitly
body: Provision 29 is the single most significant change in the 2024 Code, and the one this lesson treats most carefully, because it is not yet fully in force for most companies. Under the previous Code, boards were expected to review the effectiveness of the company's risk management and internal control systems and report that they had done so — a relatively soft, retrospective statement. Provision 29 goes further: it requires the board to monitor the company's risk management and internal control framework on an ongoing basis, and to declare, based on that monitoring, whether it considers the framework to have been effective, describing any material weaknesses identified and the actions taken.

This has been widely described as the UK's answer to the internal-controls assurance regimes seen in other jurisdictions — a meaningfully stronger obligation to actually evidence monitoring, not just assert that a review happened. It is a genuine step up in rigour, and boards, audit committees and their advisers have spent the run-up period building the monitoring frameworks needed to make an honest declaration possible.

The critical fact to hold onto: Provision 29 applies only to accounting periods beginning on or after 1 January 2026. For a company with a calendar financial year, that means its first Provision 29 disclosure appears in the annual report covering 2026, published in 2027. As at the date this lesson is written, the provision is in its final run-up phase — companies are building the necessary processes, but no full reporting cycle has yet completed under it. Treat it as a significant, well-signposted reform in the process of landing, not as settled market practice you can assume every company has already implemented.

components.definition: Requires the board to monitor the company's risk management and internal control framework and declare on its effectiveness, identifying material weaknesses and remedial action — a stronger, ongoing-monitoring obligation than the previous Code's retrospective review. Applies to accounting periods beginning on or after 1 January 2026.

interaction.prompt: How confident are you that most UK premium listed companies had already published a full annual report disclosure under Provision 29 by late September 2026?
sliderLabels: Confident — widely reported on by now
Confident — not yet, it's still phasing in
interaction.correctPosition: Confident — not yet, it's still phasing in
interaction.explanation: Not yet. Provision 29 only applies to accounting periods beginning on or after 1 January 2026, so a calendar-year company's first disclosure under it covers the 2026 financial year and would typically appear in the annual report published in 2027. As at this lesson's date, companies are preparing, not yet reporting.

parts.heading: Hard duty, soft norm: don't blur s 172 into the Code
parts.voice: reflective — closes by drawing the line the whole lesson has been building towards
body: It's tempting, after four parts on detailed Code provisions, to treat the Code as just another layer of a director's legal duties. Resist that. Companies Act 2006, s 172 — the duty to promote the success of the company — is a statutory, fiduciary duty. A director who breaches it can be sued by the company, faces the full range of breach-of-duty remedies (account of profits, equitable compensation, and so on, as covered in Lesson 9), and the duty exists whether or not the company is even listed.

The Code creates no equivalent cause of action. A shareholder cannot sue a director for breaching Provision 29, or for a board evaluation that wasn't externally facilitated when the Code said it should be. The consequence of a Code departure is reputational and market-based: a qualified 'explain' that investors find unconvincing, proxy advisers recommending votes against re-election or the remuneration report, or, in a serious governance failure, pressure that ultimately surfaces as a genuine s 172 or wider duty claim once things go wrong enough that the underlying conduct crosses into a legal breach.

The two systems reinforce each other without being the same thing. Good compliance with the Code's disclosure expectations is evidence a board is taking its statutory s 172 duty seriously; poor Code compliance is not itself unlawful, but it is often the visible symptom of governance failures that, if they get bad enough, do eventually become a legal problem.

components.commonWrongAnswer: Students often say a company 'breached the law' by failing to comply with a Code Provision.
components.whyItsWrong: Non-compliance with a Provision is not unlawful under 'comply or explain' — only the failure to disclose that non-compliance, or to explain it properly, engages the Listing Rules. The Code itself creates no statutory duty and no cause of action; s 172 and the other CA 2006 duties remain the separate, hard legal layer underneath it.

interaction.prompt: Which of these gives rise to a claim a shareholder could actually bring against a director?
interaction.scenarioA: The board fails to appoint an externally facilitated board evaluator for three consecutive years and gives only a generic, unconvincing explanation in the annual report.
interaction.scenarioB: A director diverts a corporate opportunity to a company they personally control, in clear breach of the duty to promote the success of the company and avoid conflicts of interest.
interaction.explanation: B is a breach of hard statutory duties (s 172 and the conflicts duties covered in Lesson 7), directly actionable by the company or, in limited circumstances, a shareholder via a derivative claim. A is a weak 'comply or explain' disclosure — a governance and market-confidence problem, not itself a legal wrong a shareholder can sue over.

testPool.prompt: Name the regulatory mechanism through which the UK Corporate Governance Code binds premium listed companies.
acceptableAnswers: comply or explain, via the FCA Listing Rules
testPool.modelAnswer: 'Comply or explain', operating through the FCA Listing Rules, which require disclosure of compliance or a proper explanation for departure from each Provision.

testPool.prompt: Who issues the UK Corporate Governance Code?
options: The Financial Reporting Council (FRC)
The Companies House registrar

testPool.prompt: Which of these companies is directly subject to the UK Corporate Governance Code's 'comply or explain' reporting obligation?
options: A small private family company with three shareholders
A company with a premium listing on the London Stock Exchange
Any UK company registered at Companies House
A sole trader operating as a limited company
testPool.trapExplanation: The Code's disclosure requirement is triggered by the FCA Listing Rules, which apply to premium listed companies specifically — not to every company registered at Companies House, and not to private companies regardless of size.

testPool.prompt: Put these steps in the order a company follows when it decides to depart from a Code Provision.
items: The board considers whether following the Provision suits the company's circumstances this year
The board decides a departure is justified for good, specific reasons
The annual report discloses the departure and explains the reasoning clearly to shareholders
Shareholders and proxy advisers assess whether the explanation is convincing

testPool.prompt: Under Provision 29, what must the board's declaration on internal controls describe, beyond a bare statement that the framework was reviewed?
options: Any material weaknesses identified and the actions taken in response, based on ongoing monitoring rather than a one-off retrospective look
Only whether the external auditor signed off the accounts without qualification
The individual salaries of every audit committee member
testPool.explanation: Provision 29 requires ongoing monitoring and a declaration addressing effectiveness, material weaknesses and remedial action — a materially stronger obligation than the previous Code's retrospective effectiveness review.

testPool.prompt: In this explanatory extract, highlight the sentence that most precisely states what makes an 'explain' compliant rather than a bare non-compliance statement.
testPool.passage: It is not enough for a company simply to record that it did not comply with a Provision. A proper explanation must set out the background, give a clear rationale for the board's action, and describe any mitigating steps taken and the timeframe for any intended return to compliance. A vague or generic statement of departure does not satisfy the Listing Rules' disclosure requirement.
testPool.ratioSentence: A proper explanation must set out the background, give a clear rationale for the board's action, and describe any mitigating steps taken and the timeframe for any intended return to compliance.

testPool.prompt: Tap the fact that shows this company's Provision 29 disclosure would not yet be expected under the current phasing.
testPool.scenarioText: The company has a financial year running from 1 January to 31 December. Its most recently published annual report covers the year ended 31 December 2025. The board has been building an internal controls monitoring framework throughout 2026 in preparation for future reporting requirements.
tappableSpans: financial year running from 1 January to 31 December
most recently published annual report covers the year ended 31 December 2025
building an internal controls monitoring framework throughout 2026
testPool.correctSpan: most recently published annual report covers the year ended 31 December 2025
testPool.explanation: Provision 29 applies to accounting periods beginning on or after 1 January 2026. A report covering the year ended 31 December 2025 relates to a period that began before the trigger date, so it falls outside Provision 29's scope — the first affected report will cover 2026.

testPool.prompt: Which scenario illustrates a breach of a hard statutory duty, rather than a soft governance norm?
testPool.scenarioA: A director fails to disclose a personal interest in a proposed transaction with the company, contrary to CA 2006 s 177.
testPool.scenarioB: A remuneration committee does not include a clawback provision in a new executive pay scheme and explains the omission in the annual report.
testPool.explanation: A is a breach of a statutory duty (s 177), directly actionable. B is a Code departure handled through disclosure and explanation, not a legal wrong in itself, however much shareholders may dislike the explanation given.

testPool.prompt: A premium listed company's annual report states only: 'The board did not comply with the audit committee independence provision this year.' Does this satisfy the Listing Rules' disclosure requirement?
options: No — a bare statement of non-compliance without a substantive explanation does not satisfy 'comply or explain'
Yes — any acknowledgement of non-compliance is sufficient
No — non-compliance with this Provision is never permitted under any explanation
testPool.explanation: 'Comply or explain' requires a genuine, specific explanation, not merely an admission of departure. A bare statement fails the disclosure standard even though departure from the underlying Provision is, in principle, lawful if properly explained.

testPool.prompt: A company with a financial year beginning 1 April 2026 asks whether Provision 29 applies to that year's annual report. What is the answer?
options: Yes — the accounting period begins after 1 January 2026, so Provision 29 applies to it
No — Provision 29 only applies to calendar-year companies
No — Provision 29 does not apply until 2027 regardless of financial year
testPool.explanation: Provision 29 applies to accounting periods beginning on or after 1 January 2026, regardless of a company's particular financial year end — a period starting 1 April 2026 is caught.

testPool.prompt: A premium listed company's board decides its chair should also sit on the audit committee, believing the chair's deep sector knowledge outweighs the Code's usual expectation of separation, and discloses this clearly with detailed reasoning in the annual report. A shareholder complains this is unlawful. Analyse whether the shareholder is correct.
factsToOrder: The Code's audit committee provision expects the chair not to be a member
The board departs from that expectation for a stated reason
The departure and the board's reasoning are disclosed clearly in the annual report
A shareholder alleges the departure is unlawful

scaffolds.support: Full model answer shown, mapped to Issue / Rule / Application / Conclusion
Rule given; student applies it to the facts and writes the conclusion
No scaffold; student writes the full analysis unaided

modelAnswer.issue: Whether a premium listed company acts unlawfully by departing from a Code Provision, provided the departure is disclosed and explained.
modelAnswer.rule: Under 'comply or explain', operating through the FCA Listing Rules, a company is not legally required to comply with any given Provision; it is legally required to disclose whether it has complied and, if not, to give a clear and substantive explanation.
modelAnswer.application: The board here has departed from the audit committee independence expectation but has disclosed the departure and given a clear, substantive rationale. That satisfies the Listing Rules' disclosure obligation. The departure itself is not unlawful — the shareholder may disagree with the board's judgement, but disagreement with a properly explained departure is not a legal wrong.
modelAnswer.conclusion: The shareholder is incorrect: the departure is lawful provided the disclosure and explanation are adequate, which on these facts they appear to be.

testPool.prompt: Why is it inaccurate to describe the UK Corporate Governance Code as imposing 'legal duties' on directors?
options: Because the Code's substantive Provisions are not directly enforceable as law; only the surrounding disclosure obligation is a legal requirement under the Listing Rules
Because the Code has been formally repealed
Because the Code only applies to private companies, which have no directors' duties
testPool.trapExplanation: The Code is very much in force and applies to premium listed public companies, not private ones. The precise inaccuracy is treating its substantive content as directly enforceable law — it is the disclosure requirement around it, not the underlying Provisions, that carries legal force.

testPool.prompt: Order these from the most 'hard law' obligation to the most 'soft norm' expectation.
items: A director's statutory duty under CA 2006 s 172
The Listing Rules' requirement to disclose compliance or explain departure from the Code
A specific Code Provision, such as external facilitation of board evaluation

testPool.prompt: How confident are you that a shareholder could bring a direct legal claim against a director purely for a company's non-compliant Code disclosure, with no accompanying breach of a Companies Act duty?
sliderLabels: Confident — no direct claim arises from the Code alone
testPool.correctPosition: Confident — no direct claim arises from the Code alone
testPool.explanation: Correct. The Code creates no standalone cause of action. Enforcement of poor Code compliance runs through shareholder and market pressure (voting, proxy advice, reputational cost), not litigation — unless the underlying conduct separately breaches a statutory duty such as s 172.

debriefConfig.trapSummary: The most common mistake in this lesson's test items is treating a Code Provision as if it were directly enforceable law. Remember the layering: the Listing Rules' disclosure duty is hard law; the Provisions themselves are soft norms enforced by shareholders and the market, not by a court.
